corrapa01.bio: Pat Corrales managed Cleveland from 1983 to 1987 after being fired by the first-place Phillies at the 1983 All-Star break. His Indians went 280-355 and peaked with a winning record in 1986, fifth in the AL East. In 1987 he was fired at 31-56 after a preseason Sports Illustrated cover billed the club as the best team in the majors.
quotes: Get the bunt down and move him over.
We have the speed in Butler and Franco, so let them run.
Go to the pen early when the starter is struggling.

sources.quote: No reliable verbatim Corrales quote found; SABR bio carries only quotes about him.
sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. Corrales is thinly documented; values are near league average with a mild lean to speed (Butler, Franco).

coxbo01.bio: Bobby Cox took over the Blue Jays in 1982, tied for last that year, went 89-73 in 1983, finished second in 1984, and won the club's first AL East title in 1985 with the league's best record (99-62) before losing the ALCS to Kansas City in seven games. He was AL Manager of the Year in 1985. He platooned freely (Rance Mulliniks and Garth Iorg at third) and liked to let runners go.
coxbo01.quote: I liked to turn the runners loose.
quotes: Mulliniks against the righty, Iorg against the lefty. That is how we win.
Send him. Moseby can take the base.
Stay with the starter until he shows he is done.

sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. Quote 'turn the runners loose' is SABR's account of his managing; 1980s platoon habit is general reputation (Mulliniks/Iorg).

craigro01.bio: Roger Craig took over the Giants in September 1985 when they were on pace for 100 losses, then won the NL West in 1987 and the 1989 NL pennant (92-70) before being swept by Oakland. He promoted rookies Will Clark and Robby Thompson in 1986 and taught the split-fingered fastball to his staff. His clubs hustled to the 'Humm Baby' slogan and he stayed patient with starters.
craigro01.quote: The key to it is you throw it like a fastball. You don't try to turn it over or cut it.
quotes: Humm baby. Keep the pressure on.
Stick with the starter if he is throwing the split well.
Platoon them. Everybody plays.

sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. The quote is about the split-fingered pitch, not strategy; no strategy quote located.

felskjo01.bio: John Felske managed the Phillies from 1985 until his firing on June 18, 1987 (29-32 start). In 1986 they finished 86-75, second in the NL East, 21.5 games behind the Mets. A Phillies preview quoted him on the club's speed, and he shifted Mike Schmidt back to third base in 1986.
felskjo01.quote: We had a lot of speed last year without Gary. We just didn't get on enough to use it.
quotes: Get Redus on and let him run.
Schmidt plays third every day.
Hook him when the lineup turns over a third time.

sources.quote: https://vault.si.com/vault/1986/04/14/19-philadelphia-phillies (quote reached via search snippet attributed to Felske; page not opened, treat as moderately verified)
sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. Felske's SABR bio is unassigned; tendencies are hard to document and set near average.

freyji99.bio: Jim Frey won the 1980 AL pennant with Kansas City (97-65), then lost the World Series to Philadelphia in six games; he was criticized for starting righty Rich Gale twice rather than Paul Splittorff. In 1984 he led the Cubs to 96-65 and their first division title since 1945, losing the NLCS to San Diego after winning the first two games. He was Manager of the Year in 1984.
freyji99.quote: to find out the ability of each man and try and get the top performance out of him with the ability he has.
quotes: Play the percentages. Righty against righty.
Let the club hit away and trust the big bats.
Make the pitcher work out of it, no need to get cute.

sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. Quote is how Frey described his job as a coach; style is not described in the SABR bio. Sliders near average.

gardnbi02.bio: Billy Gardner took over the Twins in 1981 after an 11-25 start and went 30-43. Minnesota had losing records in 1982 and 1983, then went 81-81 in 1984, and he was replaced by Ray Miller at 27-35 in 1985. He was a blunt, old-school manager who relied on the hit-and-run and the bunt.
gardnbi02.quote: The two words I hate most in the world are communication and motivation.
quotes: Bunt him over. Take the out.
Hit and run here. Make something happen.
Leave the pitcher in and let him finish what he started.

sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. SABR notes only that he rejected modern managing; the small-ball lean is his general reputation.

houkra01.bio: Ralph Houk managed Boston from 1981 to 1984 after earlier stints with the Yankees and Tigers, finishing with 1,619 wins and 1,531 losses over twenty years. He contended only in the second half of 1981. A former Yankee catcher, he was known for protecting his players, seldom criticizing them publicly, and knowing each pitcher's strengths.
houkra01.quote: I knew their best pitches and their worst, and when to call for speed and when to use their slower stuff.
quotes: Leave my player alone. He will get it done.
One more run and Stanley comes in.
Play the veterans. They know how.

sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. Houk's Red Sox tactics are not detailed in sources; set as a conservative veteran manager.

howsedi01.bio: Dick Howser took over the Royals on August 31, 1981, won the AL West in 1984 and 1985, and beat St. Louis in seven games for the 1985 World Series, the franchise's first. His record in Kansas City was 404-365. He stepped aside in July 1986 with brain cancer. His Royals ran and pushed the bunt and kept Dan Quisenberry as the closer.
howsedi01.quote: I just line them up and let them play.
quotes: Wilson on first, so be ready. He is going.
Let Quiz finish it.
Get the runner over and let McRae drive him in.

sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. The Royals' speed (Willie Wilson, U L Washington) is general knowledge, not in the SABR text.

johnsda02.bio: Davey Johnson managed the Mets to 90 or more wins in each of his first five seasons: 90 in 1984, 98 in 1985, 108 and the World Series in 1986, 92 in 1987, and 100 in 1988. He had played for Earl Weaver and used his roster fully, platooned, and relied on computer analysis and young players from the farm system.
johnsda02.quote: I was going to be baseball's first big-league manager to embrace sabermetrics.
quotes: Platoon them. Put the right bat in against the starter.
No bunt. Wait for the three-run homer.
Pinch-hit early; I have a full bench for a reason.

sources.quote: https://metsrewind.substack.com/p/davey-johnson-a-beautiful-mind (quote from a secondary Substack article, attributed to Johnson)
sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. Weaver-style roster use is from SABR; low bunt and platoon use are general reputation.

larusto01.bio: Tony La Russa took over the White Sox in 1979 at age 34, won the AL West in 1983 (99-63) and AL Manager of the Year, and was fired at 26-38 in 1986. He then joined Oakland, which won pennants in 1988, 1989 and 1990. In Oakland he used Dennis Eckersley almost exclusively as a ninth-inning closer, which Bill James called the most important smart move of a manager in the 1980s; he also platooned and used lefty-righty matchups.
larusto01.quote: The key is, you've got a responsibility and an opportunity to put people in the right places and try to win games.
quotes: Right-hander in, left-hander out. Match them up.
Eckersley gets the ninth with a lead. Nobody else.
Pinch-hit now; I want the better matchup.

sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. Matchup-heavy bullpen and platooning are from SABR and general reputation; lineup tinkering (pitcher batting eighth) noted by SABR.

lasorto01.bio: Tommy Lasorda won the 1981 and 1988 World Series and the 1981, 1983, 1985 and 1988 division titles; the 1985 team won 95 games and the 1988 team 94. He was criticized for heavy small ball but the criticism eased after 1988. He leaned on starting pitchers and did not build a deep bullpen.
lasorto01.quote: Ralph taught me that if you treat players like human beings, they will try to play like Superman.
quotes: Bunt him over; we play for one run.
The starter finishes what he starts.
Walk the eighth hitter and let the pitcher hit.

sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. SABR cites small ball and heavy reliance on starters; the 1981 Series walk of the eighth hitter to reach Tommy John is documented.

lillibo01.bio: Bob Lillis became Houston's interim manager in August 1982 (28-23 the rest of the way) and kept the job through 1985: 85 wins and third place in 1983, 80-82 in 1984, 83-79 in 1985. He announced 'I am not a platoon manager,' abandoning predecessor Bill Virdon's constant lineup changes, and used computer charts and radar-gun feedback in 1984.
lillibo01.quote: I am not a platoon manager.
quotes: Same lineup tonight. Nobody is platooning.
Cruz can run, so let him.
Check the chart before we make a move.

sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. Rejection of platooning is documented in SABR; Astrodome speed game is general reputation.

pinielo01.bio: Lou Piniella managed the Yankees in 1986 and 1987 (90 wins in 1986) and part of 1988 under George Steinbrenner. An intense, demanding manager, he later ordered a bunt with two strikes in the 1990 World Series and pulled Jose Rijo with a two-hitter in Game 4 for Randy Myers, showing a willingness to push his bullpen.
quotes: Get him out of there. Bring in the closer.
Squeeze the run if we have to.
Run on his first move.

sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. Quote is short and generic; no richer strategy quote was found. Yankee records not in the SABR text.

rodgebu01.bio: Buck Rodgers managed the Brewers from 1980 (division title in the strike-split 1981) until early 1982, then the Expos from 1985 to 1991. His best Montreal year was 1987, when the club won 91 games and he was Manager of the Year. As a catcher he was regarded as a strong pitch-caller; his Expos ran with Tim Raines and played with limited budgets.
rodgebu01.quote: a teacher, a motivator, someone who's fair but who will never take fairness for weakness.
quotes: Let Raines run, he reads the pitcher.
Make the move now; we need the matchup.
Be aggressive. Take the extra base.

sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. SABR gives no tactical detail; running emphasis rests on the Raines-era Expos reputation.

rosepe01.bio: Pete Rose became Reds player-manager on August 16, 1984 and managed until the 1989 ban. He finished second in the NL West four straight years (1985-88), and was suspended 30 days in 1988 for shoving an umpire. He played hard, rode hustle, and stayed loyal to veterans and relievers such as John Franco.
rosepe01.quote: I'd walk through hell in a gasoline suit to play baseball.
quotes: Hustle on every play.
Take the extra base; they will not throw you out.
Franco gets the save.

sources.quote: No manager-era quote found in SABR bio; the gasoline-suit line is a widely repeated Rose line but I did not locate a URL for it, treat as unverified
sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. Rose's tactics are not documented in the SABR bio.

tannech01.bio: Chuck Tanner won the 1979 World Series with the 'We Are Family' Pirates and managed Pittsburgh through 1985 (winning records in 1980, 1982 and 1983), then Atlanta in 1986-88. His 1976 A's stole an AL-record 341 bases and his 1977 Pirates 260; he rotated relievers one inning at a time, with Kent Tekulve, Enrique Romo and Grant Jackson. Known as 'Mr. Sunshine' for his optimism.
tannech01.quote: This may not be the end; it may be the beginning.
quotes: Send the runner. We play to win.
Go to the pen now; Tekulve is ready.
Pinch-run for him; speed wins.

sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. Running and bullpen rotation figures are in SABR; the quote was from 1978.

trebeto99.bio: Tom Trebelhorn managed Milwaukee from 1986 to 1991. In 1987 the Brewers opened 13-0, then lost 12 straight in May and finished 91-71, third in the AL East. He helped Rickey Henderson refine base stealing at Boise in 1976-77 and ran an aggressive, hustling team built around Molitor and Yount.
quotes: Go. We run on this pitcher.
Hit and run, let's keep them moving.
Pull him; we have a fresh arm.

sources.quote: No reliable verbatim Trebelhorn quote found; his SABR bio is unassigned.
sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. Poorly documented; running emphasis from the Henderson connection and the 1987 Brewers' style.

valenbo02.bio: Bobby Valentine was hired in 1985 with the Rangers 9-23 and went 53-76 the rest of the way. Texas went 87-75 and second in 1986, 75-87 in 1987, 70-91 in 1988 and 83-79 in 1989. A young manager who explained his decisions to players and remembered shouting 'We should be bunting now' as a player.
valenbo02.quote: That's why I try to let my players know my thinking.
quotes: We should be bunting here.
Run on the first move.
Charge the bunt; get the lead runner.

sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. Bunting lean rests on SABR anecdote and general reputation.

willidi02.bio: Dick Williams led the Padres to 81-81 in 1982 and 1983, then 92-70 and the 1984 NL pennant (World Series loss to Detroit in five games), and 83-79 in 1985 before being forced out. He then managed Seattle from 1986 (58-75 over the full season) until he was fired 46 games into 1987. A strict disciplinarian, he moved Rollie Fingers to relief and used pinch hitters and matchups aggressively.
willidi02.quote: I managed right along with them. I learned from every manager what to do and what not to do.
quotes: Pinch-hit now, the matchup is wrong.
Get the closer up; this is the inning.
No mistakes; execute the play.

sliders: Slider values are reputation-based judgments from the cited bio plus general 1980s coverage; no single source gives numbers. SABR does not discuss platooning or bunting by Williams; those values rest on his general reputation as a matchup-minded disciplinarian.
